utterances.text: Evening Mayor and council members in the community. I have some important updates for the council and the community about the state of homelessness in San Rafael. We are navigating some incredibly complex legal areas that have massively constrained the city's ability to enforce even our own local ordinances. So if you bear with me, I'm going to provide just a brief background if anybody's listening that doesn't know what we've been dealing with over the last year just to kind of set the stage of where we are and what what's to come. The city's been in litigation over a camping ordinance that the City Council passed last summer in August of 2023. This ordinance aimed to create a regulatory framework to help mitigate for the health and safety issues that are created by homeless encampments. An enormous amount of staff, time and energy has been spent and along with our our service providers over the last nine months responding to the court's rulings and orders and establishing a new camping ordinance that we can utilize enforcement tool when necessary, which was passed just this past March. That new camping ordinance does set maximum campsite sizes to 200 square feet for individuals and 400 square feet for more than one individual, and establishes buffer zones from schools. For example, you can't camp within 250ft of a school, within 10ft of a private property line, and 10ft from utility infrastructure. So that new ordinance is something we can implement. However, we are still in active litigation over the prior camping ordinance. This litigation that was filed against the city by the California Homeless Union follows the 2018 Supreme Court decision called Martin vs. Boise, in which the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that cities cannot criminalize a person for sleeping on public property and that the city cannot ban camping on public properties unless there are adequate shelter space available for that individual to stay, which unfortunately, we do not have enough adequate shelter here in Marin County. Recently, the Supreme Court heard arguments about a month ago regarding the related 9th Circuit ruling in Johnson vs. Grant's Pass. During these arguments, the City of San Rafael's ongoing litigation and involvement with the District Court over our own camping ordinance was referenced three times regarding the city's inability to enforce our own local regulations. We're extremely frustrated by how much this litigation and subsequent orders from the court seem to defy all logic. It's very, very difficult for us as staff to convey to the council as well as to the community why we cannot enforce our own regulations. Very recently in this last week, this city issued fire code violation notices to several illegal structures which were located, which are located along Francisco Boulevard west and directly in front of Marin Roofing Company. The fire inspectors issued these notices in direct response to a recent fire located at the encampment area which spread to the nearby fence of Marin Roofing. It damaged electrical equipment associated with a propane tank on their property. This fire could have been a catastrophic disaster if it were not for the swift responsiveness of the Sierra Fell Fire Department. This encampment continues to be a troublesome fire risk for those living there as well as for the local businesses and the community. Last week, our fire department inspected and found that the structures and camping equipment is creating a hazardous condition, an imminent fire risk for all individuals in the area, and that the encampment cannot be made safe and needs to be removed. The city had planned to conduct outreach to those individuals residing in those structures last Friday to offer them assistance with the dismantling of those structures and to provide new tents, bedding and storage of their personal items so they could move to a safer area for camp. However, the city was blocked by the federal court last Friday who ruled that while the individuals living in the structures are to relocate to tents along the Mahone Creek path tomorrow, their structures must remain in place pending the outcome of their peer appeals on encroachment right of way violations, which are scheduled to be considered at an administrative hearing on June 25th. This just this afternoon, the judge denied a request for a temporary restraining order in the city's favor, seeking to stop any immediate enforcement of our fire code. Additionally, the judge denied the city's request to fence off the structure to be vacated and is requiring the city to return to the judge to request that installation should problems arise at the site. The city desperately needs to be able to utilize our own local ordinances to keep the community safe, including both the fire code, the encroachment codes and and our camping on public property regulations. Unregulated camping can and has led to dangerous conditions, including these types of fires and other public health and safety concerns which we need the ability to mitigate. However, what we collectively struggle to reconcile is that our efforts to resolve public health and safety issues relating have been consistently met with a threat of or actual obstruction by the plaintiffs in the Boyd case through the court for references Just today the Homeless Union filed a Request for Temporary Restraining order to block the City from proceeding with the Judge's order to relocate individuals from their structures to tents along the nearby Mahone Creek Path. Luckily, the temporary restraining order was not granted. This obstruction does not come at the hands of the individuals experiencing homelessness, but rather a select few individuals who are advocates for those residing in these encampments. In light of the opposition, the City remains steadfast in our commitment to center the voices of the unhoused with empathy and compassion and bring them into problem solving and co creation of our Solving Homelessness Homelessness together. We do have an Encampment Resolution State Encampment Resolution Funds Grant which includes two phases. First to include the development of a sanctioned camping area located along the northern part of Mahone Creek path. The structured program will include dedicated property management 247 security, access to mobile showers and regular waste management services. The program is somewhat akin to our former SSA which seeks to focus resources and support to assist individuals in their pathway to housing. We are in the process of vetting contractors to provide these services and are planning for this to open later this summer. The City has an ongoing commitment to working with individuals experiencing homelessness, while we're also committed to addressing the concerns of the local business community who needs to be assured that their property ability to operate and livelihood is not upended as collateral damage to larger societal challenges that we face. So at this time there are some things that we can do and these are the things that we can do. The City is implementing its new ordinance. Over the next week.
